note:
Two things about refusing rather than reporting a bound in `look_grep`.

(1) The ordering does NOT force report-over-refuse. In the match branch (src/observe.rs:438-478) `printed.push_str(&stdout)` and the exclusion note run FIRST, before `by_file` is built and before any `PendingEntry` is constructed; the `Search` entry and the per-file `GrepMatch` entries are pushed onto the in-memory `buf` after that, and `pending::save(workspace_dir, &buf)?` is the last statement before `Ok(LookOutcome { printed })`. So an implementation that bounds while assembling `printed` reaches the bound before any entry exists and before anything is persisted, and could return `Err` there discarding nothing. Nothing in this range makes a refusal impossible.

(2) What does decide it is the crate's own report-versus-refuse discriminator, stated in `targets.rs`'s module doc (targets.rs:44-49): the census refusal is a refusal because "Here nothing is left to tell: the remedy is singular. Run the workspace-rooted grep, mint the fact, cite it — or withdraw the target", as against `scope`, which "stayed human-owed because only a person can tell context from conclusion". A whole-`src` grep for `refuse` shows every `workspace::refuse` call site in the crate is of that singular-remedy kind — a missing or malformed input, or a forbidden flag combination: claims.rs (no --proposition, no such claim, --revise without --why, unknown cited fact), facts.rs (empty note, no such fact), prose.rs (--ack combined with any of --text/--revise/--heading/--level/--cites/--before, --level out of 1..=6), targets.rs (no symbol, uncensused symbol), transplants.rs (empty --text, withdrawn ids, an unanswered premise at render), observe.rs (no such path, invalid --lines range, `--grep` without a path, `lines` with `grep`). Not one refusal anywhere in src is keyed to the size or content of a result. A byte budget is not a singular-remedy condition: the author who hits it has no act that re-runs the search under the budget.

F2 shows the crate already reasons this way: the test comment at authoring_cli.rs:508-510 justifies naming memos in the label precisely so that two differently-excluded searches "would not pin identically".

This claim's mechanism is that `printed` and the pending entries "are built separately... neither reads the other" — today true, and F1(5) confirms the `Search` label is computed from `root`, `pattern`, `by_file.len()` and `note`, none of which touch `printed`. After the change the label must carry N, a number that exists only as a product of bounding `printed`. The design therefore creates the coupling this claim says is absent, and an implementer who took the claim at face value ("a bound imposed while assembling `printed` cannot reach the buffer") would bound `printed` and leave the label alone — which is the design's own defect back again.

What survives unqualified: the captured `output`, the key and the world markers do stay byte-identical, so overlap and re-resolvability are untouched (F1(2),(3): `ExtentEntry::censuses` reads kind/pattern/key/world_root and never the label, and `scope::extent_covers` only enlarges its haystack).

The claim as written establishes only that the cut must fall on a line boundary; it does not establish that a line-boundary cut always returns something, and the design nowhere states what happens when it returns nothing. A range that merely contains an over-budget line does not reach the floor and returns no byte of that line: `--lines 12:20` on tet46 releases lines 12-14 (3 whole lines, 11852 B) and stops before line 15; `--lines 8:20` on tet46 releases 3 whole lines, 6608 B; `--lines 12:21` on tet30 releases 3 whole lines, 12855 B.

note: `run` has this ticket's defect and this design does not fix it — read so that the standing non-coverage entry can be written honestly about what it does and does not cover. (1) `run_command` (src/observe.rs:537-621) captures the child's merged stdout/stderr into one buffer, converts it with `String::from_utf8_lossy`, and then uses the same value twice: `output: output_text.clone()` into a `PendingEntry` of kind `ObservationKind::Proc` keyed by the command line and labelled `proc: {cmdline} (exit {exit_code})`, and `Ok(RunOutcome { printed: output_text, .. })` as the return. Nothing anywhere in the function measures, bounds or truncates either copy, and the label carries the command line and the exit code and no measure of size. (2) Both front ends hand that return back whole: the CLI does `print!("{}", outcome.printed)` (src/main.rs:526) and the MCP handler returns it as the `"output"` field of a structured result (src/mcp.rs:652-657), neither measuring it. (3) The `run` tool's own description (mcp.rs:649) already contemplates the large case and answers it by warning the author rather than by bounding anything: "The whole output is captured verbatim and, once minted into a fact, becomes permanently unrevisable and ships into the snapshot beside the memo — so a command whose output is enormous, or contains a credential, puts that in a repository forever." So a `run` return overruns the caller's cap exactly as an unbounded `look` return does, and the only thing standing against it today is that warning. Note the census scope here: this fact opens `run_command`, its two call sites and the `run` tool description; it is not a whole-worktree census of any symbol.

note: `look_grep` is two modes selected by whether its root is a directory, and the single-file mode leaves stdout order recoverable from the shipped ledger. `-r` is pushed only `if root_path.is_dir()` (observe.rs:361-363), and `Exclusions::decide` returns `Exclusions::None { why: "the caller named one file" }` for any non-directory root (observe.rs:252-254), so `look --grep <pattern> <one file>` is a first-class mode that searches exactly that file and applies no exclusions. `-H` is pushed unconditionally, so even in that mode every stdout line is `<file>:<lineno>:<text>`. In that mode the `BTreeMap` `by_file` has exactly one key, and its `Vec<String>` holds each matched line's `{lineno}:{text}` in stdout order (the `for line in stdout.lines()` push order), and the shipped `GrepMatch` entry's `output` is `matches.join("\n")` with label `{file} (grep: {pattern})`. So the file name, the line order and every matched line are all in the ledger, and the full grep stdout reconstructs from a single-file `GrepMatch` entry. With a directory root the same map holds many keys ordered by filename, which is not the stdout order.
